newsitem.title: UK: Protestant gunmen pivotal to peace in N.Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Protestant gunmen pivotal to peace in N.Ireland.

text.p: For 25 years their gunmen swept through Catholic neighbourhoods spraying houses and bars with bullets before declaring a 1994 ceasefire that seemed to seal an unprecedented peace in British Northern Ireland.
Now pro-British Protestant Loyalist guerrillas there hold the key to whether the province will again become a cauldron of sectarian strife.

Their arch-enemies, the Irish Republican Army, are back on the warpath. Protestant politicians say the IRA wants to trap to draw them into a bloody re-run of the strife that stalked the province for 25 years over the future of British sovereignty.

In the streets of hardline Protestant areas, where gable murals celebrate the Loyalist guerrillas' gory exploits, people say they do not want a Protestant backlash but they fear the shadowy figures behind the groups may strike.

Two IRA bombs which expoloded inside the British Army's headquarters at Lisburn, south of Belfast, on Monday -- the first in the province since the republican guerrillas ended their 17-month truce in February -- has intensified pressure on the Loyalists to draw their guns again, Loyalist sources say.

Loyalist groups, so called because of an unswerving allegiance to the British Crown, killed hundreds of Catholic Irish nationalists in areas where the IRA draws support for its campaign to end London rule and achieve a united Ireland.

The IRA's resumption of war with bombs in London in February fuelled fears that the Loyalists would scrap their own truce but they stuck to it, earning international praise for a self-restraint never previously associated with the trigger-happy killer squads.
The Loyalist Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF) has its roots in struggles for and against rule from London 80 years ago which spawned the modern IRA, Europe's best-drilled guerrilla band.

The IRA has had an unbroken existence since but the UVF was re-formed in the mid-1960s to combat nationalist demands and try to keep Northern Ireland British. The Ulster Defence Association (UDA), the Ulster Freedom Fighters (UFF) and Red Hand Commando (RHC) were formed in the early 1970s.
The four comprise the Combined Loyalist Military Command (CLMC), which controlled their sectarian onslaught and still calls the shots over whether the truce will last.

The CLMC, led by men sworn to stand fast against any move to loosen Northern Ireland's ties to London, says that the British national flag, the Union Jack, will forever fly over the province, which the IRA regards as "occupied territory".

Loyalist guerrillas believe their mission is sacred and have built up a mystique and folklore around what police say is naked sectarian murder. An underground UVF cassette of Patriotic songs by The Platoon is dedicated to "Our British Way of Life".
The UVF is thought to have about 1,000 supporters, mostly in the countryside, while the other three have bigger support centred in working-class strongholds in towns.
They have stockpiles of modern weaponry, including expertly manufactured home-made arms, and explosives expertise.
Security sources say the leaders have a political strategy but many footsoldiers are headstrong bigots who have done well out of drug dealing and racketeering and are still bent on havoc.

Irish and British security forces fear that, if Loyalists go back to war, towns in the largely Catholic Republic of Ireland might be targeted for bombs, and Catholic-owned pubs in Northern Ireland might again become scenes of carnage.
